why: Concrete, named framework with all four risks; A's 'two questions remain' header and 'three questions' text are inconsistent and it's thinner.
Personal arc gives the closing line its weight; A drops the setup so the blur has no referent.
Guess prompt comes before the reveal, so the participant actually predicts; A reveals the answer before asking.
Adds the shaping-together step and the evidence framing; B's blank-page line is thin.
Tells the reader what a mismatch means, so the spot-check ends in a conclusion.
'Session' is the course's controlled term and fits the 'one session at a time' framing; 'run' is a vocabulary slip.
Title carries the takeaway, and the closing line stays short.
A's M6 encode-loop aside and closing 'flywheel' line add unresolved referents; B is cleaner.
Dropping the 'shape the whole map has had from the start' claim removes a vague overreach.
The last line adds a clear, motivating reason to save the prompt.
'Exercise' matches what students ran; 'M6 prompts' is vaguer.
The 'No pre-made prompt:' phrasing is clearer than B's fragment, and 'this scrollback' fits the on-screen context.
B states the practitioner default plainly; A's forward reference to Module 4 adds dependency for no gain.
'The training runs on YOUR real work' is a smoother, more direct opener.
'The move is the same every time' names the pattern and gives the takeaway a hook.
B ends on the decision; A's trailing Phase 3/4 roadmap is filler for the room.
B spells out the red-green loop the agent runs, so the reader knows what the diff is.
'It's often just a draft' is tighter than 'It often isn't. It's a draft…'.
B tells the room they're only recognising the strands here, lowering load.
A gives the room a concrete viewing instruction instead of a bare 'Ask these one at a time'.
'Three new concerns' matches the three bolded items and is more concrete than 'new concerns'.
'Three pressures' matches the three bullets and is a more memorable header.
'Where the file gets read' is a clearer header for the three examples.
B's prompt line is more specific about what the third prompt surfaces, linking to MCP tools.
A's extra 'Three modules in, this is your practice now' repeats the previous sentence; B is tighter.
A is punchier and lists the full tally (ten fixes, three pushbacks), which is the story the slide says it is. B explains each number but is slower and cuts the ending.
The cut sentence only restated the heading, so B is cleaner.
A's opening bullet is a redundant, hedged fragment; B starts directly on the substance.
'Read what Claude proposes' is the natural verb; 'Check' is redundant with the verifier theme.
B states a real point, that recurring work has a shape; A's is a vague restatement of the exercise.
The title 'A check resets the chain' states the takeaway and is shorter than A's.
The imperative title tells the room what to do; A's title is just a complaint.
A's 'ccstatusline or /statusline runs it live' is confusing; B says what's oldskool and how to set up the status line.
'Written as an ADR (Architecture Decision Record)' is clearer than A's awkward 'inspect (ADR)' phrasing.
B names 'The wall', which gives the room a memorable handle for the concept.
B's title is concrete and vivid and matches the Slack-thread example; A's is abstract.
'Context window' is the term used in the body; the full name is clearer for a title.
The closing line lands the point that even good models need enforced checks.
'Five things' sets up a countable list and signals the structure.
Tells the participant what to ask Claude; A's 'spot what's generic' is vague about who does it.
The closing line corrects the likely misreading that the phases run in sequence.
The permission line lowers the barrier and fits the experiment framing.
Concrete and actionable, saying what to do in the session; A is abstract and hedged.
The connective lines orient participants and explain why each piece comes next.
Plain wording ('the change you'd make') avoids the git-flavoured 'committed change' and keeps the axes simple.
